extracted.intended_audience: lighthouse engineers, maritime safety authorities (Trinity House), naval/maritime experimenters and acoustical engineers
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental evaluation and practical design guidance for fog-signals (guns, rockets, sirens, reflectors, and explosive charges) used by lighthouses, lightships, and coast signalling. Emphasizes acoustic effectiveness, directionality, safety, cost, and environmental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapidity of combustion / promptness of shock
rubrics_metrics.description: The more rapid the shock imparted to the air, the greater is the fractional part of the energy of the shock converted into wave-motion; slow impulses fail to form distinct sound-pulses because air flows to forestall condensations/rarefactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explosive materials and charge forms giving the sharpest, most rapid conversion to gas (e.g., fine-grain powders beat coarse pebble-powder; gun-cotton detonates more rapidly than gunpowder and thus produces stronger pulses). Stokes' observations (intercepting reciprocating flow) explain why prompt impulses produce effective sound-pulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape and size of the exploding mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape and size of the exploding mass affect the constitution and intensity of the sound-wave; rectangular slabs, fragments of different sizes, and rockets yield differing wave-forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with fragmenting large slabs into smaller charges — small charges can be nearly as effective as larger ones (example measured values: 4‑oz 3.12, 6‑oz 3.34, 9‑oz 4.0, 12‑oz 4.03). Small charges (e.g., 4–12 oz) often give economy with high effectiveness; choose geometry that produces desired directivity and prevents local overconcentration of energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gun shape and muzzle design (parabolic muzzle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape of the gun (including parabolic muzzles) controls how sound is projected; a parabolic muzzle is intended to project the sound over the sea and prevent landward waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A parabolic muzzle/ specially shaped gun can increase intensity in the forward direction (seaward), as proven by the bespoke revolver-style parabolic gun built to fire 3 lb charges. However, because reinforcement in one direction implies withdrawal elsewhere, parabolic muzzles may be disadvantageous where rearward or omni-directional coverage is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reflectors (parabolic reflectors / focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing explosions in the focus of a parabolic reflector reenforces sound in a chosen direction; reflectors increase intensity in the focused sector but reduce energy elsewhere and are subject to mechanical damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflectors can make gun-cotton detonations 'unanimously pronounced loudest' in the focal direction, but reflectors may fracture under powerful explosions (they can still be effective after fracture). Use reflectors when strong directional signalling is desired and mechanical robustness is ensured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gun material (bronze vs cast-iron) and ringing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Bronze guns produce sonorous qualities (ringing) superior at short distances, while cast-iron guns can be superior at long ranges because bronze ringing withdraws energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that the vibration/ringing of bronze contributes to near-field sound but may not persist to distance; cast-iron may be preferable for long-range audibility. Further experiments recommended to confirm range-dependent superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of explosive material (gunpowder vs gun-cotton vs cotton-powder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different explosive materials vary in density and combustion rapidity; these factors influence sound intensity and propagation. Gun-cotton and cotton-powder were found experimentally often to equal or exceed gunpowder in sound production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gun-cotton detonated in a reflector clearly dominated other sources in focal tests; in some comparative trials gunpowder from an optimized parabolic gun matched gun-cotton in mean sound. Cotton-powder can yield very effective reports. Account for material cost (1 lb gun-cotton ≈ cost of 3 lb gunpowder) and handling/practical firing discipline when selecting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directionality vs omnidirectional coverage requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stations (e.g., promontories) need forward-projected sounds, while lightships and central foci need all-round distribution; devices that concentrate sound (parabolic gun/reflector) may be unsuitable for all-round coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose parabolic guns or reflectors for directed seaward signalling; prefer open explosions (gun-cotton in the open or gun-cotton rockets) for central/omnidirectional needs like lightships or points requiring rearward as well as forward propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of explosion (ground-fired vs rockets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explosions detonated at elevation (via rockets) can clear acoustic shadows, produce aerial echoes, and send sound vertically/obliquely downwards to cover wider azimuths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rockets carrying gun-cotton to ~800–1,000 ft often produced stronger or longer-range audibility at locations blocked from ground signals, and generated characteristic 'aerial echoes' with notable duration (e.g., echoes lasting ~7 seconds). Use rockets to bypass obstacles and extend range where safe and practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and atmospheric effects (wind, clouds, calm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wind direction and strength substantially affect signal propagation (sounds against the wind travel much shorter distances); atmospheric conditions affect echo behavior and audibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position observers and evaluate signals under various wind conditions. Expect sounds against the wind not to penetrate much beyond ~3 miles in some tests. Calm, serene atmospheres produce pronounced aerial echoes. Account for prevailing winds when placing directional devices or deciding between rockets and directional guns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic shadows and obstacle clearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Land, trees, cliffs, and promontory shapes can cast acoustic shadows that render ground-fired guns unheard at nearby points; elevation or rockets can overcome these shadows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When station sight-lines to sea are obstructed, prefer elevated explosives (rockets) or other methods that radiate above obstacles to reach leeward points. Experimental cases (e.g., Flamborough Head, Lundy Island) showed rockets audible where guns were hidden behind cliffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local safety and risk of damage from concussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explosions near lanterns, lighthouse structures, or ship decks may cause local mechanical damage from concussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing powerful open detonations too close to sensitive structures; consider mechanical arrangements to distance the firing-point or adopt rockets to place explosions at a safe elevated distance. Balance simplicity and effectiveness with protection of equipment and personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy vs life-safety trade-offs (cost considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative cost of materials (e.g., gun-cotton vs gunpowder) must be considered, but cost should not be stretched too far when human life is at risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While 1 lb of gun-cotton may cost as much as 3 lb of powder, effectiveness and safety can justify higher expense; experimental comparisons should include cost-per-effective-sound judgment but prioritize safety and audibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directional emission patterns of slabs/charges (orientation matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploding slabs and charges emit waves non-uniformly; the broad side of a slab can send denser waves than the edge, leading to directional differences and localized effects (e.g., cutting a suspending wire only when broad side faced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient slabs or mounted charges so their broad faces favor the intended coverage sector; test multiple orientations because small angular changes can change which direction receives greatest intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siren/whistle performance dependence on drive power and axis orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical signalling devices like sirens depend on their power source pressure and pointing: lower drive pressure or unfavorable orientation reduces effectiveness outside the axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sirens operate at designed steam/air pressures (e.g., 70 psi steam yielded better results than 30–40 psi compressed air). Point trumpets/sirens to the desired bearing; expect strong axis-lobe performance but rapid fall-off at right angles and in rear sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and evaluation methods (observer placement, ear-estimation, mean values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audibility was commonly judged by multiple human observers at various positions/distances and summarized by mean values or ear-based scales; ear-estimated numeric scales were used to express relative intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple observers at varied bearings and distances to obtain robust comparative data; be aware that ear-based scales are subjective (the article records mean values and notes that physical instruments might show different numerical trends). Record environmental conditions (wind, cloud) and use consistent reference charges for comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerial echoes and temporal signal characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevated detonations (rockets) produced 'a continuous train of echoes' that retreated and died off over seconds, extending the perceptible duration and possibly the effective detection range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both peak loudness and echo/duration characteristics when assessing signal effectiveness; echoes can enhance detectability at distance even if initial pulse attenuates.
